4.6 — Player Melee: A Hitbox That Remembers the Enemy

Every mechanic so far has happened to you. Coins came to you, spikes hurt you, turrets shot at you. Today the player acts back: a box that follows your facing, a variable that remembers what the box is touching, and a key that turns remembering into damage.

Search terms for this lesson“how do I give the player a sword swing?”Guided build
Break It Down~10 minGuided build

Every mechanic so far has happened to the player. Today it happens from the player. The shape is three pieces that look like one: a box that follows you around, a box that remembers what it is touching, and a rule that says what touching means. Get any one of the three wrong and the sword swings and nothing happens — with no error to tell you which piece.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Put a trigger box on the player where a sword would beA child Square with a BoxCollider2D that is Is Trigger, one unit on a side. A child, not a component on the root, so it can sit somewhere other than the player's centre without moving the body.Read: the trigger-versus-collision distinction from 2.1.
  2. Move that box to whichever side you are facingFour branches in the same if/else if chain that already sets facing. One block, two jobs: the string the bullet reads and the position the box sits at.Read: the facing block from 1.6.
  3. Remember what the box is touchingOnTriggerEnter2D() stores the object and OnTriggerExit2D() forgets it. That pair is the memory: at any moment, currentEnemy is either the thing in front of you or null.Read: the pickup trigger from 2.1, pointed at a moving object instead of a coin.
  4. Swing on a key, gated by the cooldown you already haveInput.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.E), cooldownTimer < 0, and currentEnemy != null. Three conditions, and all three matter: a swing with nothing in front of you must not throw.Read: the countdown timer from 3.3.
  5. write this partRead: the enemy damage method from 4.1.

Four of the five parts are shapes you have built before, which is why the lesson is not level 1. The new idea is narrow and worth naming: the player holds a reference to another object and calls a method on it. Damage is a message, not a number the player keeps.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Make a sword swing" cannot be looked up. "Call a method on the object my trigger is touching" can.

Your turn

The player calls ChangeHealth(-1) on the enemy. What would change about the design if the enemy instead asked the player "did you hit me?" every frame?

The two boxes on the player do different jobs: the root box is solid and stops you walking through walls, the child box is a trigger and lets everything through. Say what would break if you swapped them.

In the Editor ~20 min
  1. Hierarchy → select the Player → right-click → 2D Object → Sprites → Square, and name the child Square. It is a child, so it inherits the player's position every frame.
  2. Inspector → Square → Transform: set Scale to 1, 1, 1 and Position to 0, 0, 0. You are about to move this object from code, so its starting place barely matters — but its scale does, because it is the size of your sword.
  3. Inspector → Square → Add Component → Box Collider 2D, then tick Is Trigger. A trigger reports that something is inside it without pushing anything — the same choice you made for the coin in 2.1, and the opposite of the player's own collider, which is solid.
  4. Game view → press Play and watch the square. It sits on the player and follows it. Leave the sprite visible for now — you are about to move it, and a box you cannot see is a box you cannot debug.
  5. Once the walkthrough is done — Hierarchy → Player → Inspector → Player Controller → Attack Box: drag the Square in. Then Overrides → Apply All, so every Player in the project gets the same child.
  6. Game view → play, walk up to an enemy and press E. Then Hierarchy → Square → Sprite Renderer and untick it: the box still works with nothing drawn, which is what you want in a finished game.
In the Code ~20 min
APIWhat it gives youWhat it costs
other.gameObject The object behind a collider — what you store when the box touches an enemy. It is a whole object, not a component: you still have to look up what you need on it.
GetComponent() The enemy's own script, so you can call a method on it. Returns null when the object has no such component — and the next dot throws.
transform.position + new Vector3(x, y, 0) Somewhere relative to the player, recomputed every frame. It writes a world position, so it overwrites whatever the box's own Transform said.
Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.E) One swing per press, from the Input class you have used since 1.4. Held down it stays true for one frame only — which is what you want for a swing.
The game already tells the player which key this is. The Overworld's Canvas carries the text Press [E] to Interact — so the prompt you inherited and the key you are wiring today are the same key. That is not a coincidence, and it is worth keeping true: if you ever move the swing to another key, the sign on the wall has to move with it.

Socratic: Who Owns the Damage?

  1. The player calls ChangeHealth(-1) on the enemy rather than subtracting from a health number the player keeps. What does that arrangement make harder, and what does it make impossible?
  2. currentEnemy holds one object. Two enemies in the box at once, one walks away — what goes wrong, and is that acceptable for a sword?
  3. The attack box is a trigger, not a solid collider, even though a sword feels solid. What would happen to your player if you unticked Is Trigger?
In the CodeGuided build

The question this answers“how do I give the player a sword swing?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. No new script: every line today goes into the file you already have, beside the movement and the bullet. One line is left for you — the one that turns a remembered object into damage.

This build leaves 1 line for you to write. Everything around it is given, so you always know the shape of what you are producing.

Step 1Add the two fields: the box, and the memory

In the class body, next to projectile and facing.

    [SerializeField] GameObject attackBox;
    GameObject currentEnemy;
  1. 1A slot for the child you built in the editor. It is serialized because it is a reference you drag in, and it is a GameObject rather than a Transform because nothing here needs to know it is a transform.
  2. 2The memory. Not serialized, not set in the Inspector — it is null until the box touches something, and null again the moment that thing walks away.

Step 2Move the box in the block that already sets facing

You have an if/else if chain from 1.6 that decides facing. Add one line to each branch instead of writing a second chain — two chains deciding the same thing is how they start disagreeing.

        if (xDirection > 0)
        {
            facing = "Right";
            attackBox.transform.position = transform.position + new Vector3(.5f, .5f, 0);
        }
        else if (xDirection < 0)
        {
            facing = "Left";
            attackBox.transform.position = transform.position + new Vector3(-.5f, .5f, 0);
        }

        if (yDirection > 0)
        {
            facing = "Up";
            attackBox.transform.position = transform.position + new Vector3(0, 1, 0);
        }
        if (yDirection < 0)
        {
            facing = "Down";
            attackBox.transform.position = transform.position + new Vector3(0, 0, 0);
        }
  1. 3The string from 3.5 — the bullet reads it.
  2. 4The box, half a unit right and half a unit up. transform.position on the left is the box's; the one on the right is the player's, because it has no object in front of it. Adding a Vector3 to a position is a move, not a direction.
  3. 9The same offset mirrored on X.
  4. 12A separate if, not an else if. Vertical facing wins over horizontal because it is checked after it — which is what makes "up" and "down" reachable at all when both axes are pressed at once.
  5. 15One unit straight up.
  6. 20Zero offset — the box sits exactly on the player. It is the one branch that looks like a mistake, and it is not: swinging downward puts the box under you, and the player's own centre is where "under you" starts.

Step 3Remember the enemy, and forget it when it leaves

Two callbacks, the same pair you wrote for the coin in 2.1 — except the coin was destroyed on contact and this one is not.

    void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other)
    {
        if (other.gameObject.CompareTag("Enemy"))
        {
            currentEnemy = other.gameObject;
        }
    }

    void OnTriggerExit2D(Collider2D other)
    {
        if (other.gameObject.CompareTag("Enemy"))
        {
            currentEnemy = null;
        }
    }
  1. 1The same signature as the coin branch. Unity calls this on every trigger that overlaps this object — which now includes your attack box, because the box is your object's child and the collision is reported to the player.
  2. 3Only enemies. A coin inside the swing radius must not be remembered as something to hit — CompareTag() is a filter, and this is how you keep one callback from meaning two things.
  3. 5Store the object, not its health. The player has no business knowing how much health an enemy has; it only needs to know who is in front of it.
  4. 9The other half. Without it, currentEnemy would still point at the last thing you touched from anywhere on the map — and the swing would reach it across the level.
  5. 13Forget. Note that this says nothing about which enemy left: if two enemies overlap the box and one walks away, the field clears anyway. That is a real limitation of remembering one thing, and Unit 4's state work is where it gets addressed.

Step 4Swing on E — this is the blank

Four lines in Update(), below the shooting code.

        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.E) && cooldownTimer < 0 && currentEnemy != null)
        {
________________
            cooldownTimer = .5f;
        }
  1. 1Three conditions joined by &&, and all three are load-bearing. GetKeyDown = one swing per press. cooldownTimer < 0 = the same half-second the bullet pays, so you cannot swing and shoot at once. currentEnemy != null = a swing with nothing in front of you does nothing instead of throwing.
  2. Your turn3The hit, and the only line in this lesson you have not built before. currentEnemy is a GameObject. Reach into it, get its EnemyController, and call that enemy's ChangeHealth(int) with a negative amount — the signed convention from 2.7, arriving at a second kind of health. Two method calls with a dot between them.
  3. 4Reset after the hit, not before — the same order as 3.3 and 3.5.
Check your work: the finished filetry every gap first — then open this to compare

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. Three things to check: the box moves in the SAME block that sets facing, currentEnemy is cleared on exit as well as set on enter, and the swing is gated by all three conditions. The offsets are the ones in the reference build and they are not symmetric — up sits a full unit away where right and left sit half. If yours are symmetric and you prefer them, keep yours and be ready to say why.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;
// ... plus UnityEngine.SceneManagement and System, from 6.1 and 3.5 ...

public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    // ... speed, direction, animator, renderer, rb, manager, jumpsRemaining ...
    float cooldownTimer = .5f;

    GameObject currentEnemy;                 // what the sword box is touching, or null
    [SerializeField] GameObject attackBox;   // the Square child

    void Update()
    {
        // ... input, movement, gravity, jump ...

        // The facing block now does two jobs: the string the bullet reads,
        // and the position of the box the sword uses.
        if (xDirection > 0)
        {
            facing = "Right";
            attackBox.transform.position = transform.position + new Vector3(.5f, .5f, 0);
        }
        else if (xDirection < 0)
        {
            facing = "Left";
            attackBox.transform.position = transform.position + new Vector3(-.5f, .5f, 0);
        }

        if (yDirection > 0)
        {
            facing = "Up";
            attackBox.transform.position = transform.position + new Vector3(0, 1, 0);
        }
        if (yDirection < 0)
        {
            facing = "Down";
            attackBox.transform.position = transform.position + new Vector3(0, 0, 0);
        }

        cooldownTimer -= Time.deltaTime;

        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.E) && cooldownTimer < 0 && currentEnemy != null)
        {
            currentEnemy.GetComponent<EnemyController>().ChangeHealth(-1);
            cooldownTimer = .5f;
        }

        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space) && cooldownTimer < 0)
        {
            Shoot();
            cooldownTimer = .5f;
        }
    }

    void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other)
    {
        // ... the coin, potion and fireball branches from 2.1, 2.3 and 3.4 ...
        if (other.gameObject.CompareTag("Enemy"))
        {
            currentEnemy = other.gameObject;
        }
    }

    void OnTriggerExit2D(Collider2D other)
    {
        if (other.gameObject.CompareTag("Enemy"))
        {
            currentEnemy = null;
        }
    }
}
Bug Hunt: The Turret Is Not an Enemy ~10 min

Play, walk up to a turret, and press E. The Console turns red: 

NullReferenceException: Object reference not set to an instance of an object
PlayerController.OnTriggerEnter2D / Update ()

Nothing is wrong with your code. Open Hierarchy → Turret and look at two things: its Tag is Enemy, and its component list has no EnemyController on it. Your swing asked it for one, got null, and called ChangeHealth on nothing.

FixWhat it costs
Give the turret its own EnemyController with more health The turret becomes a thing you can kill — which may be exactly what you want, and is what the boss in Unit 8 assumes.
Re-tag the turret, e.g. Turret One tag, and the turret stops being hittable. Cheap, and it quietly removes a feature your game might want.
Ask first: TryGetComponent(...) One line, and nothing is broken — but you have hidden a design question behind a null check instead of answering it.
A tag is a promise, and nothing enforces it. CompareTag("Enemy") only says what an object is called. Your code then assumed that everything called "Enemy" has an EnemyController — an assumption the project does not keep. When a tag and a component disagree, decide which one is lying and fix that one.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain why the hitbox is a trigger on a child rather than a collider on the root
  • Say what currentEnemy holds between swings, and when it becomes null
  • Explain why the swing needs all three conditions, and what a missing != null costs
  • Say who owns the enemy's health, and why the player only sends a message
  • Explain the turret crash without opening the project
  • Commit and push
